name: Belief Bias
description: People can judge an argument as logically stronger when its conclusion sounds believable, and weaker when its conclusion sounds implausible, even if the formal logic says otherwise. Plausibility leaks into validity judgment.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to research readouts, strategy decks, policy arguments, and AI explanations: teams can accept a weak argument because the conclusion already feels right, or reject a valid one because the conclusion feels wrong or inconvenient.
myth_risk_note: Update 2026-09-02: the core artifact concern Dube et al. (2010) raised -- that belief bias might be a statistical artifact of inappropriate measurement models rather than a real phenomenon -- is now resolved by the same lead author's own 2018 follow-up meta-analysis, which confirms belief bias is genuine under proper hierarchical analysis. A narrower, live mechanistic question remains open (whether believability shifts a response threshold versus genuinely impairing reasoning capacity), which is why this stays at low rather than none -- but the more consequential 'is this even real' concern that originally justified a caution flag has been substantively addressed.
prevalence_note: Common in reasoning and argumentation research, and intermittently useful in product/strategy critique, but much less often named in everyday interface-design practice than more consumer-facing biases.

findings.description: In syllogistic evaluation tasks, participants' judgments were influenced by whether the conclusion sounded believable, producing belief bias even when logical validity should have been assessed independently of conclusion plausibility. The same paper found the effect was task-dependent rather than universal across every reasoning format.
findings.source_title: Belief Bias and Figural Bias in Syllogistic Reasoning
findings.source_venue: The Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology Section A
